title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
claim: A dense multi-head component is replaced by a sparse set of interpretable units that separates interactions the original entangled in superposition.
layout: 3 panels (A top-left, B bottom-left, C right), left-to-right 'Sparsify' arrows in A and B, circuit-style wiring diagram in C
description: Three lettered panels. Panel A, top: on the left, a purple, red and green stack of Multi Head Self Attention heads has colored arrows linking tokens (BOS, To, be, or, not, to) to the heads. A gray 'Sparsify' arrow leads right to a light-blue box labeled Low Rank Sparse Attention (Lorsa). That box holds many heads, mostly gray 'Inactive Lorsa Head' cards, with only a few colored ones sending arrows to tokens. Panel B, bottom-left: an MLP with four orange neurons and MHSA sit beside a residual stream. A 'Sparsify' arrow leads to a Transcoder with mostly faded neurons and a blue Lorsa block. Panel C, right: a feature-interaction diagram. Blue 'Lorsa Head 1' and green 'Lorsa Head 2' wires carry K/Q signals between feature rows, from a 'Lorsa' feature and an 'Attack' feature to a 'Superposition' output. A red Error node appears on the right. Cream feature bars hold orange circles. The eye goes first to the colorful Panel A.
caption: (A) Low-Rank Sparse Attention (Lorsa) comprises thousands of sparsely activated attention heads with 1D outputs, designed to extract interpretable attention units from the original Multi Head Self Attention (MHSA). (B) Lorsa serves as a replacement model for Transformer attention, substituting sparse interpretable components for attention modules. (C) Each Lorsa head explains an atomic feature-feature interaction across token positions, which was originally a part of an MHSA head or spread across multiple heads, i.e. put in attention superposition.
abstract: We propose Low-Rank Sparse Attention (Lorsa), a sparse replacement model of Transformer attention layers to disentangle original Multi Head Self Attention (MHSA) into individually comprehensible components. Lorsa is designed to address the challenge of attention superposition to understand attention-mediated interaction between features in different token positions. We show that Lorsa heads find cleaner and finer-grained versions of previously discovered MHSA behaviors like induction heads, successor heads and attention sink behavior (i.e., heavily attending to the first token). Lorsa and Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) are both sparse dictionary learning methods applied to different Transformer components, and lead to consistent findings in many ways. For instance, we discover a comprehensive family of arithmetic-specific Lorsa heads, each corresponding to an atomic operation in Llama-3.1-8B. Automated interpretability analysis indicates that Lorsa achieves parity with SAE in interpretability while Lorsa exhibits superior circuit discovery properties, especially for features computed collectively by multiple MHSA heads. We also conduct extensive experiments on architectural design ablation, Lorsa scaling law and error analysis.
